lead: An authoring metaphor is the tool's mental model for a title. It decides whether you build a stack of cards, a flow of icons or a timeline of layers. The choice changes how you store media, how you add interactivity and how hard a late change becomes. Card tools link screens, icon tools link objects in a flowchart, and time tools place objects on a clock. The same training title can be rebuilt in all three. Use the metaphor that matches the job: presentation, simulation or fixed playback.
prereq: You need: the media elements from Unit 4, and chapter 5.2 for the idea that software fills frames between keys.

sections.h3: Card and page tools: a stack of screens

blocks.text: An authoring metaphor is the mental model the tool gives the author. It decides where the title lives: in a stack of cards, a flow of icons or a timeline of layers. Card-based tools, also called page-based tools, treat the title as a deck of full screens. One card fills the display at a time. The author places text, images, audio and buttons on each card. A button or hot spot carries a link to another card. A menu card links to lesson cards; a quiz card links back to a lesson or forward to a score card. This is hypermedia authoring: nodes (cards) joined by links. The reader moves by clicking, not by waiting. Structure is easy to see: one box per screen. Change one card and every link to it sees the new version. Interactivity is a link: go to card 7, or if answer = B go to card 12. A card stack can branch, loop and skip. The cost is that every screen is separate; a small change to a shared banner must be repeated unless the tool has a master page.

sections.h3: Icon and object tools: a flowchart of objects

blocks.text: Some syllabi call these flowchart tools. Icon-based tools show the title as a diagram. Each icon is an object: a display, a sound, a video, a decision, a calculation. The author drags icons onto a flowline and connects them with arrows. Double-clicking an icon opens its properties: file, position, duration, trigger. Media files live in a warehouse or cast, a central store. The flowline is the program: start → show video → ask question → if correct go to praise, else go to hint. This flowchart authoring suits simulations because a decision icon can read learner input and choose the next path. A simulation is not a fixed sequence; it reacts. The icon graph also makes reuse easy: one icon can point to a shared media object, so replacing that object updates every use. The cost is that a large graph becomes a tangle; you need naming and grouping. Interactivity is expressed as control flow between icons, not as a button on a page.

sections.h3: Time-based tools: layers on a clock

blocks.text: Time-based tools organise the title on a timeline. The screen is split into layers, like transparent sheets. Each layer holds objects: background, text, video, sound. The playback head moves left to right in seconds. A frame is one instant; a keyframe marks a change. The author sets where an object starts, how long it stays and what it does. This is close to video editing. The tool knows clock time: at 12.0 s the video starts, at 18.5 s the caption appears. A cast holds reusable objects. Change the cast member and all its instances update. Interactivity is a button or a pause point that jumps to another frame, but the main structure is linear. A time-based rebuild of a branching quiz loses the branches unless the tool adds separate timelines or scenes.

blocks.where: T is total play time in seconds; N is the number of screens or cards; d is the display time per screen in seconds.

blocks.text: For 19 screens at 30 s each, T = 570 s = 9.5 min.

Choose by the job. A card tool suits a catalogue, a presentation or a course with clear screens and many links. An icon tool suits a simulation, a game-like drill or a process with decisions. A time tool suits a demo, a title sequence or a narrated lesson that plays in order. Cross-platform authoring publishes one project to desktop, web and mobile. The project keeps one structure; the tool adapts window size, input and file packaging. You do not redraw the title three times. Use card tools for interactive presentations, icon tools for virtual learning modules and simulations, and time tools for fixed demonstrations. Some syllabi call page-based tools hypermedia authoring and icon-based tools flowchart authoring. A simulation is the sharp test: it must react to learner input, so the author needs a graph or a script, not a fixed strip of frames.

figure.caption: Each box is one full screen; the dashed arrows are the learner jumping backwards, which a card stack allows and a plain video does not.

spec.title: A card-based training title
spec.aria: A card flow from menu card to lesson card to quiz card to score card, with dashed return links for a wrong answer and for going home.

examples.question: A training title has 1 menu card, 12 lesson cards, 5 quiz cards and 1 score card. How many cards does the card-based version need, and how long is the same content if rebuilt as a time-based title with 30 s per card?
steps: Count every screen: N = 1 menu + 12 lessons + 5 quizzes + 1 score.
The time-based rebuild plays each card as one screen of 30 s. Use T = N × d.
Convert to minutes: 570 ÷ 60 = 9.5 min. This assumes all screens play once; the branching of the quiz is lost unless separate scenes are added.
examples.answer: The card-based version needs 19 cards; the time-based rebuild runs 570 s, or 9.5 minutes.
examples.check:
menu = 1
lesson = 12
quiz = 5
score = 1
cards = menu + lesson + quiz + score
seconds_per_card = 30
total_seconds = cards * seconds_per_card
print(cards)
print(total_seconds)
print(total_seconds / 60)

traps: Calling icon-based tools GUI icon tools — the icons are objects on a flowchart, not toolbar buttons.
Thinking time-based means the tool has a clock. Every tool has a clock; time-based means the main structure is a timeline in seconds.
Rebuilding a branching title as a timeline and forgetting the branches disappear; the fixed sequence plays every screen once.
Counting only lesson cards in a card title; the menu, quizzes and score are cards too, and all of them take play time.
Treating cross-platform as three separate projects; it is one project with output adapted to each device.

quiz.q: What is a card-based authoring tool?
quiz.a: A tool that builds a title as a stack of full-screen cards joined by links; one card shows at a time.

quiz.q: Why does an icon-based tool suit a simulation better than a time-based tool?
quiz.a: Its decision icons read learner input and choose the next path, so the title reacts; a timeline mainly plays a fixed sequence.

quiz.q: A page-based title has 1 menu card, 8 lesson cards, 4 quiz cards and 1 score card. At 45 s per card, what is the total play time in minutes?
Compare ease of change for a shared logo in card and icon tools.
quiz.a: In a card tool the logo must be repeated on every card unless a master page exists. In an icon tool the logo is one warehouse object; replacing it updates every icon that points to it.

quiz.q: Which metaphor fits a quiz that branches on each answer: card, icon or time? Give one reason.
quiz.a: Card or icon. A card can link to different cards; an icon decision can choose the next path. A plain timeline plays a fixed order.
One project is published to desktop, web and mobile. The structure stays one project; window size, input and file packaging are adapted.

quiz.q: Why does a time-based rebuild of a branching quiz lose branching?
quiz.a: A timeline is ordered by clock time. Branches need separate scenes or jumps; without them the fixed sequence plays every screen once.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern tools blend the three metaphors: a web course builder shows pages, a logic graph and a timeline in one window. Game engines use a scene graph plus a timeline for cutscenes, and node editors are icon tools for shader and logic design. Search for hypermedia authoring, flowchart authoring, cross-platform e-learning authoring and scenario-based simulation authoring.
